poets.name: Beowulf Poet
poets.credit: No portrait exists; the poet's identity and even century of composition are unknown.
bio: The author of Beowulf is unknown — an anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet whose single surviving epic, composed in Old English somewhere between the 8th and early 11th centuries, is the longest and most celebrated poem to survive from that period.

The poem survives in one manuscript, the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv), damaged by fire in 1731 and now held by the British Library. It tells of the Geatish hero Beowulf's battles with the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, in old age, a dragon.

This text is the 1910 verse translation by the American philologist Francis Barton Gummere, prepared for the Harvard Classics and long in the public domain; it preserves the original's alliterative, four-stress line.

poets.name: John Gower
poets.credit: Photograph of Gower's tomb effigy, Southwark Cathedral — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Gower (c. 1330–1408) was an English poet, a friend and contemporary of Chaucer, who wrote major long works in all three literary languages of his day: French (Mirour de l'Omme), Latin (Vox Clamantis), and English (Confessio Amantis).

A man of some property in Kent, he spent his later years at the Priory of St Mary Overie in Southwark, where his elaborate tomb, with its painted effigy resting its head on his three books, still stands in what is now Southwark Cathedral.

Confessio Amantis, his English masterwork, frames some hundred and forty tales as a lover's confession to a priest of Venus, moving through the Seven Deadly Sins toward a final meditation on age and the end of love — dedicated, in its first version, to Richard II.

poets.name: William Langland
poets.credit: No authenticated portrait of Langland survives; his very identity is a scholarly inference from the poem itself and a single manuscript note.
bio: William Langland is the name traditionally given to the presumed author of Piers Plowman, one of the great alliterative poems of medieval England, on the strength of a fifteenth-century manuscript note naming a “William de Langlond” as its maker.

Little is known of his life beyond what can be inferred from the poem: he seems to have received a clerical education, lived for a time in London, and moved in the world of minor clergy and the poor rather than the court.

Piers Plowman survives in three successive versions (the A, B, and C texts), which Langland appears to have revised and expanded over some twenty years. It follows a dreamer, Will, through a series of visions in search of Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a sweeping allegorical satire of fourteenth-century church and society.

poets.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
poets.credit: Portrait of Geoffrey Chaucer (manuscript detail) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was an English poet, civil servant, and diplomat, widely called the father of English poetry for demonstrating that the vernacular could carry the full weight of serious literary art.

He served in the royal household under three kings, worked as a customs official and clerk of the king's works, and travelled on diplomatic missions to France and Italy, where he likely encountered the work of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.

His masterwork, The Canterbury Tales, left unfinished at his death, gathers a fellowship of pilgrims riding to Canterbury and telling stories in turn — a panorama of medieval English society in verse of astonishing variety and wit. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, in the corner that later became Poets' Corner.

poets.name: Gawain Poet
poets.credit: No portrait exists; the poet's name is unknown.
bio: Known also as the Pearl Poet, this anonymous author wrote in a north-west Midlands dialect of Middle English in the late fourteenth century, a contemporary of Chaucer working in a very different, alliterative tradition.

Four poems in a single surviving manuscript (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x) are usually attributed to this one poet on grounds of dialect, style, and shared concerns: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness (also called Purity). Nothing certain is known of the poet's identity.

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the best known of the four, is a chivalric romance and moral test of a Round Table knight, told with intricate structure and a rare sensitivity to the turning of the seasons.

poets.name: John Lydgate
poets.credit: Portrait of John Lydgate (illuminated manuscript) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Lydgate (c. 1370–c. 1451) was a Benedictine monk of Bury St Edmunds and, in his own lifetime, probably the most prolific and widely read poet in England — his surviving output runs to well over a hundred thousand lines.

He wrote in conscious imitation of Chaucer, whom he revered as his master, producing enormous works such as the Troy Book and the Fall of Princes alongside occasional verse, saints' lives, and courtly dream visions for patrons that included the royal house of Lancaster.
Modern taste has generally preferred Chaucer's economy to Lydgate's copiousness, but he was central to how English poetry was read and valued through the fifteenth century.

poets.name: William Dunbar
poets.credit: Portrait of William Dunbar — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Dunbar was a Scottish makar (court poet) attached to the household of King James IV, celebrated for the range and metrical virtuosity of his verse.
His poems move between satire, comic invective, and devotional lyric, and include the famous elegy ‘Lament for the Makers,’ with its refrain ‘Timor Mortis conturbat me.’

poets.name: John Skelton
poets.credit: Portrait of John Skelton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Skelton was an English poet and tutor to the young Prince Henry, later Henry VIII, remembered for the idiosyncratic short-lined verse form later called ‘Skeltonics.’
He wrote both courtly lyrics of praise and sharp satire of clergy and court, and was crowned poet laureate by three universities.

poets.name: Stephen Hawes
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Stephen Hawes was an English poet who served as a groom of the chamber to Henry VII, best known for his allegorical romance ‘The Pastime of Pleasure.’
His verse bridges medieval allegory and the new humanism of the early Tudor court, and he was among the last English poets to write in the tradition of Chaucer and Lydgate.

poets.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Thomas Wyatt — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Thomas Wyatt was a Kentish courtier and diplomat under Henry VIII, credited with introducing the sonnet form into English poetry after his travels in Italy.
His lyrics of love and court intrigue circulated in manuscript during his lifetime and were first printed posthumously in Tottel’s Miscellany (1557).

poets.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, was an English nobleman and poet who, alongside his friend Sir Thomas Wyatt, helped pioneer the English sonnet and was the first to write English verse in blank verse.
He was executed for treason in the last weeks of Henry VIII’s reign, at the age of twenty-nine.

poets.name: Alexander Scott
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alexander Scott was a Scottish court poet whose surviving work, some three dozen short lyrics, chiefly concerns love and courtly compliment.
Little is known of his life beyond scattered records connecting him to Inchmahome Priory and the Scottish court of Mary, Queen of Scots.

poets.name: George Gascoigne
poets.credit: Portrait of George Gascoigne — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Gascoigne was an English soldier, courtier and poet whose ‘A Hundreth Sundrie Flowres’ (1573) is considered one of the first substantial collections of original English verse and prose.
He also wrote what is often called the first original prose comedy in English and an early treatise on the art of English versification.

poets.name: Alexander Montgomerie
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Montgomerie — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Montgomerie was a Scottish Jacobean courtier and makar, master poet at the court of James VI, best known for the allegorical dream-poem ‘The Cherrie and the Slae.’
A Catholic at a Protestant court, he later fell from royal favour over his religion and political dealings.

poets.name: Nicholas Breton
poets.credit: Portrait of Nicholas Breton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nicholas Breton was a prolific English poet and prose writer of the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods, admired for pastoral lyrics such as ‘Phillida and Coridon.’
He wrote across a remarkable range of genres, from devotional verse to satire, over a career of some fifty years.

poets.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Walter Raleigh was an English courtier, explorer and poet, a favourite of Elizabeth I who later fell from favour and was ultimately executed under James I.
His surviving poems, several written while imprisoned in the Tower of London, meditate with stoic clarity on time, fortune and mortality.

poets.name: Edmund Spenser
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Spenser — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Spenser was an English poet best known for his epic ‘The Faerie Queene,’ but he also wrote a substantial body of shorter verse, including the pastoral ‘Shepheardes Calender,’ the sonnet sequence ‘Amoretti,’ and the wedding hymns ‘Epithalamion’ and ‘Prothalamion.’
He spent much of his career in Ireland as a colonial administrator, and his poetry stands at the centre of English Renaissance literature.

poets.name: Christopher Marlowe
poets.credit: Portrait of Christopher Marlowe — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christopher Marlowe (1564-1593) was an English poet and dramatist, the most celebrated of the University Wits and the leading figure of Elizabethan tragedy before Shakespeare.

Alongside his plays he left a body of non-dramatic verse, including the unfinished mythological poem Hero and Leander and a translation of Ovid's Amores, and was killed in a Deptford tavern brawl at twenty-nine.

poets.name: William Shakespeare
poets.credit: Portrait of William Shakespeare — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) was an English poet and playwright from Stratford-upon-Avon, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language.
Beyond his plays, his non-dramatic verse includes the 154 Sonnets, the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, and the shorter pieces collected as The Passionate Pilgrim.

poets.name: Ben Jonson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ben Jonson — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ben Jonson (1572-1637) was an English poet and playwright, the dominant literary figure of the Jacobean stage and a rival and friend of Shakespeare.

Beyond his comedies and tragedies, he wrote a substantial body of lyric and occasional verse, including epigrams and elegies collected here from a posthumous volume of his poems and prose "Discoveries."

poets.name: Sir Philip Sidney
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Philip Sidney · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586) was an English poet, courtier, and soldier, killed at the Battle of Zutphen at thirty-one.
His sonnet sequence Astrophel and Stella (1591) is the first great sequence in English, chronicling an unrequited, thinly-veiled autobiographical love.

poets.name: Fulke Greville
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke (1554–1628), was an English poet and statesman, the close friend and biographer of Philip Sidney.
His philosophical sequences, published posthumously as Certaine Learned and Elegant Workes, weigh monarchy, religion, and human frailty in dense, difficult verse.

poets.name: Samuel Daniel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Daniel (1562–1619) was an English poet and historian, admired for the plain, measured elegance of his style.
His sonnet sequence Delia and the narrative poem The Complaint of Rosamond made his early reputation.

poets.name: Michael Drayton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Drayton (1563–1631) was an English poet whose vast body of work spans the sonnet sequence Idea, historical verse, and the topographical epic Poly-Olbion.
His Barons' Wars retells the civil strife of Edward II's reign in stately ottava rima.

poets.name: William Drummond of Hawthornden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Drummond of Hawthornden (1585–1649) was the first considerable Scottish poet to write in English rather than Scots.
His polished sonnets and elegies were shaped by his wide reading in French and Italian verse.

poets.name: John Donne
poets.credit: Portrait of John Donne by Isaac Oliver · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was an English poet and cleric, the foremost of the metaphysical poets.
His verse — by turns erotic, witty, and devout — moved from the love poems of his youth to the religious sonnets of his years as Dean of St Paul's.

poets.name: George Herbert
poets.credit: Portrait of George Herbert · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and priest, a central figure of the metaphysical school.
His single collection, The Temple (1633), published just after his death, gathers the devotional lyrics for which he is loved.

poets.name: Thomas Carew
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Carew survives.
bio: Thomas Carew (1595–1640) was an English Cavalier poet at the court of Charles I, admired for the polish of his amorous lyrics.
His Poems (1640) circulated widely and shaped the courtly style later followed by Lovelace and Suckling.

poets.name: Sir John Suckling
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Suckling (1609–1641) was an English Cavalier poet and courtier, famed for his wit and his invention of the card game cribbage.
His collected verse, Fragmenta Aurea (1646), mixes light, conversational love lyrics with plays and prose.

poets.name: Sir William Davenant
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Davenant · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Davenant (1606–1668) was an English poet and playwright who served as Poet Laureate from 1638. A bridge between the ages of Shakespeare and Dryden, he helped reopen and reshape the English theatre after the Restoration.
His most ambitious work is the unfinished heroic poem Gondibert (1651); the collection Madagascar; with Other Poems (1638) gathers his courtly and occasional verse.

poets.name: Henry King
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry King (1592–1669) was an English poet and Bishop of Chichester.
He is remembered above all for ‘The Exequy,’ his elegy for his young wife — one of the great grief poems of the century.

poets.name: John Milton
poets.credit: Portrait, Christ’s College, Cambridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and polemicist, author of the epic Paradise Lost. He went blind in mid-life and composed his greatest work by dictation.
Though he predates the Romantic movement, his blank verse and his figure of Satan shaped nearly every English poet who followed.

poets.name: Richard Crashaw
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Crashaw survives.
bio: Richard Crashaw (1613–1649) was an English metaphysical poet known for the ecstatic, ornate devotion of his sacred verse.
A convert to Catholicism, he collected his poems as Steps to the Temple (1646), consciously following George Herbert.

poets.name: Abraham Cowley
poets.credit: Portrait of Abraham Cowley by Sir Peter Lely · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was among the most celebrated English poets of his century, a child prodigy admired for his metaphysical wit.
His 1656 Poems gathers odes, elegies, and the love sequence The Mistress.

poets.name: Richard Lovelace
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of this collection's engraving survives in the public record used here.
bio: Richard Lovelace (1617–1657) was an English Cavalier poet who fought and was imprisoned for the Royalist cause.
Best remembered for ‘To Althea, from Prison’ and ‘To Lucasta, Going to the Wars,’ his posthumous Lucasta volumes appeared in 1659.

poets.name: William Habington
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Habington (1605–1654) was an English poet whose single collection, Castara (1634), celebrates — unusually for the age — his courtship and marriage to one woman.

poets.name: Sir John Denham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Denham (1615–1669) was an English poet best known for Cooper's Hill (1642), a landscape meditation that founded the English topographical poem.
His couplets were much admired by Dryden and Pope for their balance and control.

poets.name: Thomas Randolph
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Randolph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Randolph (1605–1635) was an English poet and dramatist, a celebrated wit at Cambridge and an adopted ‘son’ of Ben Jonson.
He died at twenty-nine; his collected Poems appeared three years later.

poets.name: Edmund Waller
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Waller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Waller (1606–1687) was an English poet and politician whose smooth, regular couplets influenced the coming Augustan style.
He wrote equally fluent verse for both sides of the Civil War, a flexibility that shadowed his reputation.

poets.name: Sir Charles Sedley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Charles Sedley (1639–1701) was an English Restoration poet, playwright, and courtier known for his wit and libertine reputation at the court of Charles II.

poets.name: George Wither
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Wither (1588–1667) was a prolific English poet and pamphleteer whose early verse, collected as Juvenilia, made him one of the most popular poets of his generation before his turn to satire and religious controversy.

poets.name: Robert Herrick
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Herrick · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Herrick (1591–1674) was an English poet and clergyman, the most prolific of the Cavalier poets.
His single vast collection, Hesperides (1648), moves between pagan celebration, courtly love, and country ritual — over a thousand short poems in one book.

poets.name: Andrew Marvell
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Marvell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Marvell (1621–1678) was an English metaphysical poet and politician.
Celebrated for lyrics such as ‘To His Coy Mistress’ and ‘The Garden,’ most of his poems appeared posthumously in the Miscellaneous Poems of 1681.

poets.name: Henry Vaughan
poets.credit: Title-page emblem from Silex Scintillans (1650) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Vaughan (1621–1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet and physician who styled himself ‘the Silurist.’
He is best known for the sacred poems of Silex Scintillans (1650), written under the deep influence of George Herbert.

poets.name: Katherine Philips
poets.credit: Portrait of Katherine Philips · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Katherine Philips (1632–1664), called ‘the Matchless Orinda,’ was an English poet and translator.
She was admired above all for her poems of female friendship; her collected Poems appeared in 1664 and 1667.

poets.name: William Blake
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1807) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker, largely unrecognised in his lifetime and now seen as a seminal figure of the Romantic age.
He engraved and hand-coloured his own illuminated books, most famously Songs of Innocence and of Experience, where word and image are inseparable.

poets.name: William Wordsworth
poets.credit: ‘Wordsworth on Helvellyn’ by Benjamin Robert Haydon (1842) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was an English Romantic poet who, with Coleridge, launched the movement in Lyrical Ballads (1798).
He made ordinary life and the natural world his subject, and served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

poets.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Coleridge at age 42 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) was an English poet, critic, and philosopher, co-founder of the Romantic movement.
His visionary poems ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ and ‘Kubla Khan’ remain touchstones of the imagination he spent his life theorising.

poets.name: Matthew Arnold
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Arnold · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Arnold (1822–1888) was an English poet and cultural critic, Professor of Poetry at Oxford.
His poems — among them ‘Dover Beach’ and ‘The Scholar-Gipsy’ — register the anxious loss of religious certainty at the heart of the Victorian age.

poets.name: Robert Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Browning (1812–1889) was an English poet and playwright, master of the dramatic monologue — a poem spoken entirely in an invented character's voice.

This selection gathers his early collections Dramatic Lyrics (1842) and Dramatic Romances (1845); his stage plays and longer closet-dramas (Pauline, Paracelsus, Sordello, Pippa Passes) are not included here.

poets.name: Lord Byron
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1813) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron, 1788–1824) was an English Romantic poet and satirist, one of the most celebrated — and scandalous — figures of his age.
He died at Missolonghi while supporting the Greek war of independence, and gave his name to the brooding ‘Byronic hero.’

poets.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poets.credit: Portrait by Alfred Clint · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English Romantic poet, radical in politics and idealist in temper.
Author of ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Ode to the West Wind,’ he drowned off the Italian coast before his thirtieth birthday.

poets.name: John Keats
poets.credit: Portrait by William Hilton (c. 1822) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet whose odes are among the most celebrated in the language.
He trained as a surgeon before devoting himself to poetry, and died of tuberculosis in Rome at just twenty-five.

poets.name: Lionel Johnson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lionel Johnson (1867–1902) was an English poet and critic associated with the Rhymers' Club and the Decadent movement of the 1890s.
A convert to Catholicism, his spare, disciplined verse turned repeatedly to faith, monastic ideals, and the pull of dissipation he struggled against.

poets.name: Oscar Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Oscar Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet, playwright, and wit, one of the most celebrated figures of Victorian literary London before his 1895 trial and imprisonment.
His early verse is lush and Romantic in the Keatsian mode, while The Ballad of Reading Gaol, written after his release from prison, is a stark, plainspoken account of suffering and remorse.

poets.name: Thomas Hardy
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Hardy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) is best known as a novelist, but after finishing Jude the Obscure in 1895 he devoted the rest of his long career chiefly to poetry.
His verse is plain-spoken and often bleak, preoccupied with chance, loss, rural Wessex life, and the death of his first wife Emma, which produced some of his most admired elegies.

poets.name: William Ernest Henley
poets.credit: Portrait of William Ernest Henley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Ernest Henley (1849–1903) was an English poet and editor whose leg was amputated in youth after tubercular illness, an experience recorded directly in his sequence In Hospital.
He is best remembered for Invictus, and his robust, muscular verse and criticism made him an influential figure among younger writers of the 1890s.

poets.name: A. E. Housman
poets.credit: Portrait of A. E. Housman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: A. E. Housman (1859–1936) was an English classical scholar and poet whose reputation rests on two slim volumes, A Shropshire Lad (1896) and Last Poems (1922).
His terse, ballad-like lyrics of doomed youth, soldiering, and rural England were composed in a private grief masked by classical restraint.

poets.name: Andrew Lang
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Lang · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Lang (1844–1912) was a Scottish man of letters, folklorist, and translator, remembered today chiefly for his coloured Fairy Books but also a prolific poet.
His verse favours French forms revived by the 1870s ballade craze, along with translations and tributes to French and English poets he admired.

poets.name: Amy Levy
poets.credit: Portrait of Amy Levy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Amy Levy (1861–1889) was an English poet and novelist, among the first Jewish women to study at Cambridge, who took her own life at twenty-seven.
Her poems of London street life, unrequited love, and urban melancholy anticipate the modern lyric's compression and irony.

poets.name: George MacDonald
poets.credit: Portrait of George MacDonald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George MacDonald (1824–1905) was a Scottish minister turned author, celebrated for fantasy novels such as Phantastes and The Princess and the Goblin, and a lifelong writer of devotional and reflective verse.
His poems return often to faith, fatherhood, nature, and the soul's struggle toward trust in a loving God.

poets.name: George Meredith
poets.credit: Portrait of George Meredith · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Meredith (1828–1909) was an English novelist and poet whose sonnet sequence Modern Love (1862) gave unusually candid, ironic voice to a marriage's collapse.
His nature poetry, especially The Lark Ascending, prizes close observation and intellectual vigour over conventional sentiment.

poets.name: William Morris
poets.credit: Portrait of William Morris · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Morris (1834–1896) was an English designer, socialist, and poet, a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle whose vast output includes the narrative cycle The Earthly Paradise and the Icelandic-inspired epic Sigurd the Volsung.
In later years his political convictions produced the direct, rallying verse of Chants for Socialists and The Pilgrims of Hope.

poets.name: Henry Newbolt
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Newbolt · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Newbolt (1862–1938) was an English poet best known for patriotic and naval verse such as Vitài Lampada and Drake's Drum, written to celebrate duty, empire, and the sea.
His confident public rhetoric made him one of the most widely recited poets of the pre-1914 era.

poets.name: Arthur O'Shaughnessy
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur O'Shaughnessy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur O'Shaughnessy (1844–1881) was an English poet who worked as a herpetologist at the British Museum while publishing richly musical, melancholy verse.
His Ode, beginning "We are the music makers," is his most famous poem and a manifesto for the visionary power of artists.

poets.name: Algernon Charles Swinburne
poets.credit: Portrait of Algernon Charles Swinburne · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was an English poet notorious in his own day for the sensuous, metrically dazzling, and often scandalous verse of Poems and Ballads.
An ardent republican, he also wrote fervent political verse cheering Italian unification and liberty, alongside a huge later output of odes, elegies, and sonnets.

poets.name: Francis Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Thompson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Thompson (1859–1907) was an English poet who spent years destitute and addicted to opium on the streets of London before his talent was discovered and he found refuge among Catholic friends.
His best-known poem, The Hound of Heaven, describes a soul fleeing and finally yielding to divine pursuit.

poets.name: Lewis Carroll
poets.credit: Portrait of Lewis Carroll · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lewis Carroll, the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), was an Oxford mathematician best known for the Alice books, whose fondness for nonsense and wordplay also produced a distinctive body of comic and whimsical verse.
The Hunting of the Snark and the parodies collected in Phantasmagoria remain classics of English nonsense poetry.

poets.name: Rudyard Kipling
poets.credit: Portrait of Rudyard Kipling · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was an English author born in Bombay, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, whose verse gave voice to soldiers, machines, and the British imperial experience in vigorous, ballad-like rhythms.
Poems such as If—, Gunga Din, and Recessional made him one of the most quoted poets in the English language.

poets.name: Alice Meynell
poets.credit: Portrait of Alice Meynell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Meynell (1847–1922) was an English poet, essayist, and suffragist, admired in her lifetime for the precision and restraint of her devout, closely observed lyrics.
A convert to Catholicism, she wrote often of motherhood, nature, and quiet spiritual attention.

poets.name: Arthur Hugh Clough
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Hugh Clough · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–1861) was an English poet and close friend of Matthew Arnold, whose verse candidly registers the Victorian crisis of religious faith and doubt.
His long poems Amours de Voyage and The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich experiment with conversational, unglamorous realism unusual for their time.

poets.name: Ernest Dowson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Dowson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Dowson (1867–1900) was an English poet of the 1890s Decadent movement, associated with the Rhymers' Club, who died of tuberculosis and drink at thirty-two.
His hallmark is a wistful, musical melancholy, most famous in the refrain "I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion," from his poem Non Sum Qualis Eram.

poets.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
poets.credit: Portrait of Alfred, Lord Tennyson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was Poet Laureate of Great Britain for over four decades and the most popular and representative poet of the Victorian age.
His work ranges from the intimate grief of In Memoriam A.H.H., written for a dead friend, to the martial narrative verse of Enoch Arden and the ballad-like Maud.

poets.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Elizabeth Barrett Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861) was one of the most celebrated English poets of her day, an invalid for much of her youth who eloped to Italy with fellow poet Robert Browning in 1846.
Her Sonnets from the Portuguese, written to Robert during their courtship, remain her best-loved work, alongside socially engaged narrative poems on slavery, child labour, and women's lives.

poets.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante Gabriel Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828–1882) was an English poet and painter, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, who worked in sister arts of image and verse throughout his career.
His sonnet sequence The House of Life traces the arc of love and loss with dense, jewelled imagery, while The Blessed Damozel imagines a dead woman watching for her lover from heaven.

poets.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Louis Stevenson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) was a Scottish novelist and poet, best known for Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, who also wrote widely loved verse.
A Child's Garden of Verses captures the imaginative world of childhood, while Songs of Travel, mostly written in his final years in Samoa, turns to restlessness, distance, and mortality.

poets.name: Charles Kingsley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Kingsley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Kingsley (1819–1875) was an English clergyman, novelist, and poet, remembered as a children's author for The Water-Babies and as a muscular-Christian social reformer.
His poems range from the classical narrative Andromeda, written in unrhymed hexameters, to plain-spoken ballads and songs of the sea and English rural life.

poets.name: Edward Lear
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Lear · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Lear (1812–1888) was an English artist and writer who, alongside a career as a natural history and landscape painter, invented much of the English nonsense verse tradition.
His limericks, alphabets, and songs such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, collected across several Book of Nonsense volumes, delight in invented words and gentle absurdity.

poets.name: Jean Ingelow
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean Ingelow · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean Ingelow (1820–1897) was an English poet and novelist, immensely popular in her lifetime, admired for narrative ballads and devotional lyrics of home, sea, and childhood.
Her poem The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire (1571), a ballad of a great flood, remained a schoolroom favourite for generations.

poets.name: Edward FitzGerald
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward FitzGerald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883) was an English writer whose free translation and adaptation of the medieval Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyam, The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
Reworked by FitzGerald through several editions, its meditations on wine, transience, and fate gave English verse a strikingly fatalistic, epicurean voice unlike anything else in the period.

poets.name: Coventry Patmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Coventry Patmore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Coventry Patmore (1823–1896) was an English poet best known for The Angel in the House, a long narrative sequence idealizing married domestic love that became one of the era's most influential, and later most contested, poems.
A convert to Catholicism, his later odes turn toward mystical and religious themes.

poets.name: Adelaide Anne Procter
poets.credit: Portrait of Adelaide Anne Procter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Anne Procter (1825–1864) was an English poet and social activist, a devout Catholic and one of the best-selling poets of the Victorian era after Tennyson himself.
Her collection Legends and Lyrics gathers narrative ballads and devotional verse, often concerned with charity, suffering, and quiet endurance.

poets.name: Emily Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Brontë · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Brontë (1818–1848) is best known as the author of Wuthering Heights, but she also wrote intense, visionary lyric poetry, much of it set in the imagined world of Gondal she created with her sister Anne.

Published pseudonymously as "Ellis Bell" alongside her sisters' verse in 1846, her poems of longing, imprisonment, and the moors were far better received by contemporary critics than the sisters' novels first were.

poets.name: Christina Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Christina Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was an English poet of devotional intensity and quiet formal mastery, sister of the painter-poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
Best known for ‘Goblin Market’ and the carol ‘In the Bleak Midwinter,’ she also wrote Sing-Song (1872), a book of nursery rhymes for children.

poems.title: Sonnet 1
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
LOuing in trueth, and fayne my loue in verse to show,
That the deere Shee, might take some pleasure of my paine:
Pleasure might cause her reade, reading might make her know,
Knowledge might pittie winne, and pittie grace obtaine.
I sought fit wordes, to paint the blackest face of woe,
Studying inuentions fine, her wittes to entertaine,
Oft turning others leaues, to see if thence would flowe,
Some fresh and fruitfull showre, vpon my Sunne-burnt braine.
But wordes came halting out, wanting inuentions stay,
Inuention Natures childe, fledde Stepdames studies blowes:
And others feete, still seem'de but straungers in my way,
Thus great with Childe to speake, and helplesse in my throwes,
Byting my tongue and penne, beating my selfe for spite:
Foole saide My muse to mee, looke in thy heart and write.

poems.title: Sonnet 2
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
NOt at first sight, nor with a dribbing shot,
Loue gaue the wound, which while I breath will bleede:
But knowne, worth did in tract of time proceede,
Till by degrees it had full conquest got.
I sawe and lik'd, I lik'd but loued not,
I lou'd, but did not straight what Loue decreede:
At length to Loues decrees, I first agreede.
Yet with repining at so partiall lot.
Now euen that foot-steppe of lost libertie
Is gone, and now like slaue borne Muscouite:
I call it praise to suffer tyrannie,
And nowe imploy the remnant of my wit
To make my selfe beleeue that all is well,
While with a feling skill I paint my hell.

poems.title: Sonnet 3
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
LEt Dainty wittes cry, on the Sisters nine,
That brauely maskt, their fancies may be tolde:
Or Pinders Apes flaunt in their phrases fine,
Enameling their pride with flowers of golde.
Or els let them in stately glorie shine,
Ennobling new founde tropes, with problemes old:
Or with straunge similes, inricht each line,
Of hearbes or beasts, which Inde or Affricke hold.
For me in sooth, no Muse but one I know,
Phrases and Problemes from my reach doe growe,
And straunge things cost too deere for my poore sprites,
How then? euen thus, in Stellas face I reede,
What loue and beauty be, then all my deede.
But coppying is, what in her nature writes.

poems.title: Sonnet 4
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
VErtue (alas) now let me take some rest,
Thou set'st a bate betweene my loue and me:
If vaine loue haue my simple soule opprest,
Leaue what thou lik'st, and deale thou not with it.
Thy Scepter vse in some olde Catoes brest,
Churches and Schooles are for thy seat most fit:
I doe confes, (pardon a fault confest,)
My mouth too tender is for thy hard bit.
But if that needes, thou wilt vsurping bee
That little reason that is left in mee.
And still the effect of thy perswasions prooue,
I sweare, my heart such one shall shew to thee,
That shrines in flesh so true a deitie.
That Vertue, thou thy selfe shalt be in loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 5
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
It is most true, what wee call Cupids dart,
An Image is, which for our selues we carue:
And fooles adore, in Temple of our hart,
Till that good God make church and Churh-men starue.
It is most true, that eyes are bound to serue
The inward part: and that the heauenly part
Ought to be King, from whose rules who doth swerue,
Rebels to nature, striue for their owne smart.
True that true beautie vertue is indeede,
Whereof this beautie can but be a shade,
Which Elements with mortall mixture breede,
True that on earth we are but Pilgrimes made.
And should in soule, vp to our Country moue:
True and most true, that I must Stella loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 6
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
SOme Louers speake, when they their Muses entertaine
Of hopes begott, by feare, of wot not what desires,
Of force of heauenly beames, infusing hellish paine;
Of lyuing deathes deere woundes, faire stormes and flashing fyres.
Some one his songes in Ioue and Ioues straunge tales attyres,
Bordered with Bulles and Swannes, poudered with golden raine:
An other humbler witte to shepheards pipe retyres,
Yet hiding royall blood, full oft in Rurall vaine.
To some a sweetest plaint a sweetest stile assordes,
Whiles teares poure out his inke, and sighes breath out his wordes.
His paper pale despaire, and paine his penne doth moue.
I can speake what I feele, and feele as much as they,
But thinke that all the mappe of my state, I display.
When trembling voice bringes foorth, that I do Stella loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 7
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WHen nature made her chiefe worke, Stellas eyes,
In collour blacke, why wrapt she beames so bright?
Would she in beamy blacke like Painter wise,
Frame daintiest lustre mixte with shaddowes light?
Or did she els that sober hewe deuise,
In obiect best, to strength and knitt our sight:
Least if no vaile these braue beames did disguise,
They Sun-like would more dazell than delight.
Or would she her miraculous power shewe,
That whereas blacke seemes Beauties contrarie,
Shee euen in blacke doth make all Beauties flowe:
But so and thus, she minding Loue should bee
Plaste euer there, gaue him this mourning weede:
To honour all their deathes, who for her bleede.

poems.title: Sonnet 8
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
LOue borne in Greece, of late fled from his natiue place,
Forst by a tedious proofe, that Turkish hardned harts
Were no fit markes, to pearce with his fine pointed darts:
And pleasd with our soft peace, staide here his fleeting race.
But finding these colde climes, too coldlie him imbrace,
Not vsde to frosen lippes, he straue to finde some part
Where with most ease and warmth, he might imploy his art.
At length himselfe he pearch'd in Stellas face,
Whose faire skinne, beamie eyes, like morning Sunne in snowe:
Deceiu'd the quaking boy, who thought from so pure light,
Effects of liuelie heate in nature needes must growe.
But she most faire, most colde; made him there take his flight
To my close hart; where while some fire brands he did lay,
He burnt vnwares his winges, and cannot fly away.

poems.title: Sonnet 9
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
QVeene Vertues Court, which some call Stellas face,
Prepar'd by Natures cheefest furniture:
Hath his front built of Alablaster pure,
Golde is the couering of that statelie place.
The doore, by which sometimes runnes forth her grace
Red Porphire is, which locke of Pearle makes sure:
Whose Porches rich, with name of chekes indure,
Marble mixt red and white, doe enterlace.
The Windowes now, through which this heauenly guest
Lookes on the world, and can finde nothing such,
Which dare claime from those sightes the name of best,
Of touch they are, that without touch doe touch,
Which Cupids selfe, from Beauties mine did drawe:
Of touch they are, and poore I am their strawe.

poems.title: Sonnet 10
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
REason, in faith thou art well seru'd, that still
Would'st brabling be, with sence and loue in me:
I rather wish thee climbe the Muses hill,
Or reach the fruite of Natures chiefest tree;
Or seeke heauens course, or heauens vnusde to thee:
Why should'st thou toyle, our thornie grounde to till?
Leaue sence and those that sences obiectes be,
Deale thou with powers, of thoughts leaue thou to will.
But thou wouldst needes fight both with Loue and sence,
With sworde of witte, giuing woundes of dispraise:
Till downe right blowes did foyle thy cunning fence,
So soone as they strake thee with Stellas rayes.
Reason, thou knewst, and offered straight to proue
By reason good, good reason her to loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 11
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
IN truth oh Loue: with what a boyish kinde
Thou doost proceede, in thy most serious waies;
That when thy heauen to thee his best displaies,
Yet of that best thou leau'st the best behinde.
That like a Childe that some faire booke doth finde
With gilden leaues of colloured Velom, playes
Or at the most on some faire picture staies,
But neuer heedes the fruite of Writers minde.
So when thou sawest in Natures cabinet,
Stella, thou straight lokest babies in her eyes:
In her chekes pit, thou didst thy pitfall set,
And in her brest to peepe, a lowting lyes.
Playing and shining in each outward part:
But foole seekst not to get into her hart.

poems.title: Sonnet 12
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
CVpid because thou shin'st in Stellas eyes,
That from her lookes thy dimnesse nowe scapes free:
That those lips swelde so full of thee they be.
That sweet breath maketh oft the flames to rise,
That in her brest thy pap well sugred lyes,
That grace euen makes thy gracious wrongs; that she,
What word so ere shee speakes, perswades for thee:
That her cleere voice, lifteth the Sunne to Skyes.
Thou countest Stella thine, like those whose powres
Hauing got vp a breach, (by fighting well)
Cry victory, this happy day is ours:
Oh no, her heart is such a Cytadell.
So fortified with wit, stor'd with disdaine:
That to winne it, is all the skill and paine.

poems.title: Sonnet 13
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
PHoebus was Iudge, twixt Ioue and Mars in loue,
Of those three Gods whose armes the fairest weare:
Ioues golden shielde, did Eagle Sables beare.
Whose talents holde young Ganimede aboue.
But in verde fieldes, Mars beares a golden Speare,
Which through a bleeding heart, his point did shoue:
Each had his Crest, Mars carried Venus gloue.
Ioue on his Helme the Thunder bolte did reare.
Cupid then smiles, for on his crest there lyes
Stellas fayre haire, her face he makes his shielde:
Where Roses gules, are borne in siluer fielde.
Phoebus drewe wide the Curtaine of the skyes
To blase the last, and swore deuoutly then:
The first thus macht, were scarcely Gentlemen.

poems.title: Sonnet 14
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
ALas, haue I not paine enough my friend,
Vppon whose breast, a fiercer gripe doth tyre,
Than did on him, who first stole downe the fyre;
While Loue on me, doth all his quiuer spend,
But with your rubarbe wordes you must contend,
To greeue me worse in saying, that desier
Doth plunge my well form'd soule, euen in the mier
Of sinfull thoughtes, which doe in ruine ende.
If that be sinne which doth the manners frame,
Well stayed with trueth, in worde and faith of deede,
Readie of wit, and fearing nought but shame;
If it be sin which in sixt hart dooth breede,
A loathing of all loost true chastitie;
Then loue is sin, and let me sinfull bee.

poems.title: Sonnet 15
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
YOu that doe search for euery purling spring,
Which from the rybs of old Pernassus flowes,
And euery flower (not sweete perhaps) which growes
Neere there about, into your Poems wring.
You that doe dictionary method bring
Into your rymes, running in ratling rowes,
You that old Petrarchs long deceased woes
With new borne sighes, and wit disguised sing;
You take wrong wayes, those far-fet helps be such,
As doe bewray a want of inward tutch,
And sure at length stolne goods doe come to light.
But if both for your loue and skill you name,
You seeke to nurse at fullest brest of Fame,
Stella behold and then begin to write.

poems.title: Sonnet 16
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
IN nature apt to like, when I did see
Beauties which were of many Carrects fine,
My boyling spirits did thether then incline,
And Loue I thought that I was full of thee;
But finding not those restles flames in me
Which others said did make theyr soules to pyne,
I thought those babes of some pins hurt did whine:
By my loue iudging what loues pains might be.
But while I thus with this young Lyon plaid,
Myne eyes (shall I say curst or blest) beheld
Stella: now she is nam'de, neede more be sayd?
In her sight I a lesson new haue speld.
I now haue learnd loue right, and learnd euen so,
As they that beeing poysoned, poyson know.

poems.title: Sonnet 17
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
HIs mother deere Cupid offended late,
Because that Mars grew slacker in her loue,
With pricking shot he did not throughly moue
To keepe the place of their first louing state:
The boy refusde, for feare of Marses hate;
Who thretned stripes, if he his wrath did proue:
But she in chafe him from her lappe did shoue,
Broke bowe, broke shaftes, where Cupid weeping sate,
Till that his Grandam Nature pittying it,
Of Stellas browes, made him two better bowes:
And in her eyes of arrowes infinit.
O how for ioye he leapes, ô how he crowes;
And straight therewith, like wagges new got to play:
Falls to shrewde turnes, and I was in his way.

poems.title: Sonnet 18
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WIth what strange checkes I in my selfe am shent,
When into Reasons Audit I doe goe:
And by such counts my selfe a Banckerowt know
Of all those goods which heauen to me hath lent,
Vnable quite, to pay euen Natures rent,
Which vnto it by birth-right I doe owe:
And which is worse, no good excuse can showe,
But that my wealth I haue most idly spent,
My wit doth waste, my knowledge bringes forth toyes,
My wit doth striue, those passions to defende
With my rewarde, the spoile of vaine annoyes;
I see my course, to loose my selfe doth bende.
I see and yet no greater sorrowe take
Than that I loose no more for Stellas sake.

poems.title: Sonnet 19
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
ON Cupids bowe, how are my hart strings bent?
That see my wracke, and yet imbrace the same:
When most I glory, then I feele most shame;
I willing run, yet when I runne repent;
My best wittes still their owne disgrace inuent,
My verie yncke, turnes straight to Stellas name:
And yet my wordes (as them my penne doth frame)
For though she passe all things, yet what is all
That vnto me, that fare like him that both
Lookes to the skyes and in a ditch doth fall,
O let me proue my mind yet in his grouth
And not in nature, for best fruites vnfit;
Scholler saith Loue bend hitherward thy wit.

poems.title: Sonnet 20
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
FLy, flye my friendes, I haue my deathes wound, flye;
See there that boy, that murthering boy I say,
Who like a thiefe hid in a bush doth lye,
Tyll blooddy bullet get him wrongfull pray.
So, tyrant he no fitter place could spy,
Nor so farre leuell in so secrete stay:
As that sweete blacke which walles thy heauenly eye,
There he himselfe with his shot close doth laye.
Poore passenger, passe now thereby I did,
And staid to see the prospect of the place,
While that black hue from me the bad guest hid,
But straight I saw motions of lightnings grace,
And there discried the glisterings of his dart:
But ere I could flie thence, it pearst my hart.

poems.title: Sonnet 21
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
YOur words my freends me causelesly doe blame,
My young minde marde whō Loue doth menace so:
That my owne writings like bad seruants shew
My wits, quick in vaine thoughts, in vertue lame;
That Plato I haue reade for nought, but if he tame
Such coltish yeeres; that to my birth I owe
Nobler desires: least els that to my foe
Great expectation were a trayne of shame.
For since mad Mars great promise made to me,
If now the May or my yeeres much decline,
What can be hop'd my haruest time will be,
Well said, your wit in vertues golden myne
Digs deepe with learnings spade: now tell me this,
Hath this world ought so faire as Stella is?

poems.title: Sonnet 22
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
IN highest way of heauen the Sunne did ride,
Progressing from fayre Twynns in golden place,
Hauing no maske of Clowdes before his face,
But streaming forth of his heate in chiefest pride,
When some faire Ladies by hard promise tyde,
On horsebacke met him in his furious race,
Yet each prepar'de with Fannes well shading grace,
From that foes wounds their tender skinnes to hide.
Stella alone, with face vnarmed marcht,
Either to doe like him, as carelesse showne:
Or carelesse of the welth, because her owne.
Yet were their hid and meaner beauties parcht,
Her daintiest bare went free; the cause was this,
The Sunne that others burnt, did her but kisse.

poems.title: Sonnet 23
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
THe curious wits, seeing dull pensiuenes
Bewray it selfe in my long setled eyes:
When these same fumes of mellancholie rise,
With idle paines and missing paines doth gesse;
Some that know how, my spring I did adresse,
Deeme that my Muse some fruite of knowledge plyes:
Others, because the Prince my seruice tryes,
Thinke that I think, State errors to redresse;
But harder Iudges, iudge ambitious rage,
(Scourge of it selfe, till clyming slippery place)
Holds my young braine captiu'd in golden cage.
O fooles, farre otherwise alas the case;
For all my thoughts haue neither stop nor start,
But onely Stellas eyes, and Stellas hart.

poems.title: Sonnet 24
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
RIch fooles there be, whose base and filthy hart,
Lyes hatching still the goods wherein they flow:
Damning themselues to Tantalus his smart,
Welth breeding want, more rich, more wretched grow.
Yet to those fooles, heauen doth such wit impart,
As what their hands doe hold, their heads doe know.
And knowing loue, and louing lay apart,
As scattered things, farre from all dangers show.
But that rich foole, whom by blinde Fortunes lot,
The richest gem of loue and life enioyes,
And can with foule abuse such beauties blot:
Let him depriued of sweet, but vnfelt ioyes
Exilde for aye, from those high treasures which
He knowes not grow, in onely follie rich.

poems.title: Sonnet 25
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
THE wisest scholler of the wight most wise,
By Phoebus doome, with sugred sentence sayes:
That vertue if it once meete our eyes,
Strange flames of loue it in our soules would rayse.
But for that man with paine this truth discries,
While he each thing in sences ballance wayes,
And so, nor will nor can behold those skyes,
Which inward Summe to heroicke minds displaies.
Vertue of late with vertuous care to stir
Loue of himselfe, take Stellas shape, that hee
To mortall eyes might sweetly shine in her.
It is most true, for since I did her see,
Vertues great beautie in her face I proue,
And finde defect; for I doe burne in loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 26
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
THough duskie wits doe scorne Astrologie,
And fooles can thinke those lampes of purest light.
Whose number waies greatnes eternitie.
Promising wondrous wonders to inuite,
To haue for no cause birth-right in the skyes.
But for to spangle the blacke weedes of Night,
Or for some braue within that Chamber hie,
They shold still daunce to please a gazers sight.
For me I nature euery deale doe know,
And know great causes, great effects procure,
And know those bodies high, raigne on the low.
And if these rules did fall, proofe makes me sure,
Who oft bewraies my after following case,
By onely those two starres in Stellas face.

poems.title: Sonnet 27
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
BEcause I oft in darke abstracted guise,
Seeme most alone in greatest company,
With dearth of words, and aunswers quite awry,
To them that would make naked speech arise;
They deeme, and of their doome the rumor flies,
That poyson foule of bubling pride doth lie
So in my swelling brest, that onely I
Faune on my selfe, all others doe dispise:
Yet pride (I thinke) doth not my soule possesse,
(Which lookes too oft in this vnflattering glasse)
But one worse fault, ambition I confesse,
That makes me oft my best freendes ouer-passe,
Vnseene vnheard, while thought to highest place
Bends all his powers, euen vnto Stellas grace.

poems.title: Sonnet 28
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
YOu that with allegories curious frame
Of others children changlings vse to make,
With me those paines for God-sake doe not take,
I list not dig so deepe for brasen fame.
When I see Stella, I doe meane the same
Princesse of beautie, for whose onely sake,
The raynes of loue I loue, though neuer slake;
And ioy therin, though Nations count it shame:
I begge no subiect to vse eloquence,
Nor hidden waies to guide Philosophie,
Looke at my hands for no such quintessence,
But know that I in pure simplicitie,
Breathe out the flames which burne within my hart,
Loue onely leading me into this arte.

poems.title: Sonnet 29
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
LIke some weake Lords neighbours by mighty kings,
To keepe themselues and their chiefe Citties free
Doe easily yeelde, that all theyr coast may be
Readie to serue their Campe of needfull things:
So Stellas hart finding what power Loue brings,
To keepe it selfe in life and libertie,
Doth willing graunt that in the Frontire he
Vse all to helpe his other conquerings.
And thus her hart escapes, but thus her eyes
Serue him with shot, her lips his Herralds are,
Her brests his Tents, legges his tryumphall Chare,
Herselfe his foode, her skin his Armor braue.
But for because my chiefest prospect lyes
Vpon the coast, I am giuen vp for a slaue.

poems.title: Sonnet 30
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WHether the Turkish new Moone minded be,
To fill her hornes vppon the Christian coast,
How Polands King mindes without leaue of hoast,
To warme with ill made fire cold Musconie,
If French can yet three parts in one agree,
What now the Dutch in their full diets boast,
How Holland harts, now so good Townes are lost,
Wherewith my Father made it once halfe tame,
If in the Scottish Court be weltering yet;
These questions busie wits to me do frame:
I combered with good manners, aunswere doe,
But know not how, for still I thinke on you.

poems.title: Sonnet 31
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WIth how sad steps ô Moone thou clim'st the skyes,
How silently, and with how meane a face,
What may it be, that euen in heauenly place,
That busie Archer his sharpe Arrowes tryes?
Sure if that long with loue acquainted eyes
Can iudge of loue, thou feelst of Louers case,
I reade within thy lookes thy languisht grace.
To mee that feele the like, my state discries.
Then euen of fellowship ô Moone tell me,
Is constant loue deemde there but want of wit?
Are beauties there, as proude as heere there be?
Doe they aboue, loue to be lou'd, and yet
Those Louers scorne, whom that loue doth possesse?
Doe they call vertue there vngratefulnesse?

poems.title: Sonnet 32
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
MOrpheus the liuely sonne of deadlie Sleepe,
Witnes of life to them that liuing die:
A Prophet oft of hidden mysterie;
A Poet eake as humors flye and creepe:
Since thou in me so sure a hold doost keepe,
That neuer I with clos'd vp sence doe lye,
But by thy worke, my Stella I discry,
Teaching blind eyes both how to smile and weepe;
Vouchsafe of all acquaintance this to tell,
Whence hast thou Iuorie, Rubies, Pearle, and Golde,
To shew her skin, lips, teeth, and head so well?
(Foole aunswers he) no Indes such treasures hold,
But from thy hart, while my Sire charmeth thee,
Sweete Stellas Image I doe steale to me.

poems.title: Sonnet 33
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
I Might, vnhappy word, (woe me) I might,
And then would not, or could not see my blisse:
Tyll now, wrapt in a most infernall Night,
I finde, how heauenly day (wretch) did I misse;
Hart rent thy selfe, thou doost thy selfe but right.
No louely Paris made thy Helen his,
No force, no fraude, robd thee of thy delight,
No Fortune of thy fortune Author is;
But to my selfe, my selfe did giue the blow,
While too much wit forsooth so troubled me,
That I respects for both our sakes must showe.
And could I not by rysing morne fore-see,
How faire a day was neere, (ô punisht eyes)
That I had beene more foolish, or more wise.

poems.title: Sonnet 34
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
COme let me write, and to what end? to ease
A burthened hart, (how can words ease, which are
The glasses of thy daily vexing care?)
Oh, cruell fights well pictured forth doe please.
Art not asham'd to publish thy disease?
Nay, that may breede my fame, it is so rare,
But will not wise men thinke thy words fonde ware?
Then be they close, and they shall none displease,
What idler thing than speake and not be heard?
What harder thing than smart and not to speake?
Peace foolish wit, with wit my wit is marde;
Thus write I while I doubt to write, and wreake
My harmes in ynkes poore losse, perhaps some finde
Stellas great power, that so confus'd my minde.

poems.title: Sonnet 35
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WHat may words say? or what may words not say,
Where truth it selfe must speake like flattery?
Within what boundes can one his lyking stay,
Where Nature doth with excellence agree?
What Nestors counsell can my flames allay,
Since Reasons selfe doth blow the coles to me?
And ah, what hope that hope should once see day,
Where Cupid is sworne page to Chastitie;
Honour is honoured, that thou dost possesse
Him as thy slaue, and now long needie Fame
Doth euen grow rich, meaning my Stellas name;
Wit learnes in thee perfection to expresse,
Not thou by praise, but praise in thee is raised,
It is a praise, to praise where thou art praysed.

poems.title: Sonnet 36
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
STella, whence doth these newe assaults arise,
A conquerd, yeelding, ransackt hart to win?
Whereto long since, through my long battred eyes,
Whole Armies of thy beauties entred in,
And there long since, Loue thy Lieuetenant lyes,
My forces raz'd, thy banners rais'd within;
Of conquest what doe these effects suffise,
But wilt new warre vppon thine owne begin,
With so sweet voyce, and by sweet nature so,
In sweetest strength, so sweetly skild withall,
In all sweet stratagems sweete Arte can shew:
That not my soule which at thy foote did fall
Long sithence forst by thy beames; but stone nor tree
By sences priuiledge can scape from thee.

poems.title: Sonnet 37
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
THus night while sleepe begins, with heauie wings
To close mine eyes, and that my troubled thought
Doth fall to stray, and my chiefe powers are brought
To leaue the scepter of all subiect things,
The first that straight my fancies errour brings
Vnto my minde, is Stellas Image, wrought
By Loues owne selfe, but with so curious draught,
That she mee thinks not onely shines but sings:
I start, looke hart, harke, but what inclos'd vp sence
Was helde, in open view it flyes away,
Leauing me nought but wayling eloquence.
I seeing bitter sights in sighes decay,
Cald it anew, and woed Sleepe againe,
But him her hoast her vnkind guest had slaine.

poems.title: Sonnet 38
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
COme Sleepe, ô Sleepe, the certaine knot of peace,
The bathing place of wits, the balme of woe,
The poore mans wealth, the prysoners release,
The indifferent Iudge betweene the hie and lowe,
With shielde of proofe, shielde me from out the presse
Of these fierce dartes, Dispayre at me doth throw;
O make in me those ciuill warres to cease:
I will good trybute pay if thou doe soe.
Take thou of me smooth pillowes, sweetest bed,
A chamber deafe of noyse, and blinde of light,
A rosie garland, and a wearie head.
And if these things (as being thine in right)
Mooue not thy heauie grace, thou shalt in mee
(Liuelier then els) rare Stellas Image see.

poems.title: Sonnet 39
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
AS good to write, as for to lie and groane,
O Stella deere, how much thy power hath wrought,
That hast my minde now of the basest brought,
My still kept course while others sleepe to moane;
Alas if thou, the height of Vertues throane,
Canst but vouchsafe the influence of a thought,
Vpon a wretch which long thy grace hath sought,
Way then by thee how I am ouerthrowne;
And then thinke thus, although thy beautie be
Made manifest, by such a victorie,
Yet noblest Conquerers doe wreaks auoide;
Since then thou hast so farre subdued me,
That in my hart I offer still to thee,
O doe not let thy Temple be destroide.

poems.title: Sonnet 40
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
HAuing this day, my horse, my hand, my Launce
Guided so well, that I obtaind the prize,
Both by the iudgement of the English eyes,
And of some sent by that sweet enmie Fraunce,
Horsmen my skill in horsmanship aduaunce,
Towne folke my strength: a daintier Iudge applies
His praise to slight, which from good vse doth rise:
Some luckie wits, impute it but to chaunce:
Others, because from both sides I doe take
My blood, from them that doe excell in this,
Thinke Nature me a man at Armes did make.
How farre they shoote awry; the true cause is,
Stella lookt on, and from her heauenly face,
Sent forth her beames, which made so faire a race.

poems.title: Sonnet 41
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
O Eyes, which doe the Spheres of beautie moue,
Whose beames all ioyes, whose ioyes all vertues be:
Who while they make Loue conquer, conquer Loue,
The Schooles where Venus hath learnd Chastitie;
O eyes, where humble lookes most glorious proue,
Onely loue tasting of your crueltie.
Doe not, doe not, from me, poore me, remoue,
Keepe still my Zenith, euer shine on me;
For thoughts eye neuer sees them, but straight waies
My life forgets to nourish languisht sprights:
Yet still on me (ô eyes) dart downe your rayes;
And if from Maiestie of sacred Lights
Oppressing mortall sence, my death proceede:
Wreckes tryumphs best, which Loue hie set doth breed.

poems.title: Sonnet 42
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
FAire eyes, sweet lips, deere hart, that foolish I
Could hope by Cupids helpe, on you to pray:
Since to himselfe he doth your gifts apply,
As his maine force, chiefe sport, and easefull stay.
For when he will see who dare him gainesay,
Then with those eyes he lookes, loe by and by,
Each soule doth at Loues feete his weapons lay,
Glad if for her he giue them leaue to die.
When he will play, then in her lips his eye,
Where blushing red, that Loues selfe them doe loue,
With either lip he doth the other kisse;
But when he will for quiets sake remoue
From all the world, her hart is then his roome:
Where well he knowes, no man to him can come.

poems.title: Sonnet 43
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
MY words I know doe well sette forth my minde,
My minde, bemones his sence of inward smart:
Such smart may pittie claime of any hart;
Her hart, sweete hart, is of no Tygers kinde,
And yet she heares, and I no pittie finde,
But more I cry, lesse grace she doth impart;
Alas, what cause is there so ouerthwart,
That Noblenes it selfe makes thus vnkinde?
I much doe gesse, yet finde no truth but this,
That when the breath of my complaints doe touch
Those daintie doores vnto the Court of Blisse,
That once come there, the sobs of my annoyes,
Are metamorphos'd straight to tunes of ioyes.

poems.title: Sonnet 44
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
STella oft sees the very face of woes
Painted in my bewrinckled stormie face:
But cannot skill to pittie my disgrace;
No though the cause heereof herselfe she knowes.
Yet Hermes late, a Fable who did show,
Of Louers neuer knowne, (a pittious case)
Pittie thereof got in her breast such place,
As from her eyes, a Spring of teares did flow.
Alas, if Fancie drawne by fained things,
Though false, yet with free store more grace doth breede
Then Seruants wreck, where new doubt honor bringes,
Than thinke my Deere, that in me you doe reede
Of Louers ruine some sad Tragaedie:
And if not me, pittie the tale of me.

poems.title: Sonnet 45
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
I Curst thee oft, I pittie now thy case,
Blinde hitting Boy, since shee that thee and me
Rules with a becke, so tyranniseth thee,
That thou must want or foode or dwelling place;
For she protests to bannish thee her face.
Her face (ô Loue) a roge then should'st thou bee,
If Loue learne not alone to loue and see,
Without desire to feede of further grace.
Alas poore wagge, that now a Scholler art
To such a Schoole-mistris, whose lessons new
Thou needes must misse, and so thou needes must smart;
Yet deere, let me this pardon get of you,
That he so long may sport him with desire,
Till without Fuell, thou can make hote fire.

poems.title: Sonnet 46
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WHat, haue I thus betraide my libertie,
Can those blacke beames, such burning markes engraue
In my free side, or am I borne a slaue,
Whose necke becomes such yoke of tyrannie?
Or want I sence to feele my miserie,
Or spirit, disdaine of such disdaine to haue,
Who for long faith some gentle pittie craue,
Yet get no almes, but scorne of beggerie.
Vertue awake, beautie but beautie is;
I may, I must, I can, I will, I doe
Leaue following that which it is gaine to misse,
Let her goe: soft, but there she comes, goe to,
Vnkind I loue you, not, (woe me) that I
Must make my hart thus giue my tongue the lye.

poems.title: Sonnet 47
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
SOules ioy, bend not those morning starres from me,
Where vertue is made strong by beauties might,
Where loue is chastnes, scorning youthes delight,
And humblenes is linckt with maiestie;
What euer may ensue, ah let me be
Copartner of the ritches of that sight:
Let not mine eyes be blinded from that light;
Oh looke, oh shine, ô let me die and see,
For though I oft my selfe of them bemone,
That through my hart their beamie darts be gone,
Whose curelesse woundes euen nowe most freshly bleede;
Yet since my deaths wound is already got,
Deere killer, spare not thy sweete cruell shot,
A kinde of grace it is to kill with speede.

poems.title: Sonnet 48
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
I On my horse, and Loue on me doth trie
Our horsmanship, while two strong works I proue,
A horsman to my horse, a horse to Loue;
And now mans wrongs in me poore beast discry.
The raines wherewith the ryder doth me tie
Are reuerent thoughts, which bit of reuerence moue,
Curbde in with feare, but with gilt bosse aboue
Of hope, which makes it seeme faire to the eye:
The wande is will, thou fancie saddle art,
Girt fast by memory; and while I spurre
My horse, he spurres with sharpe desires my hart,
He sits me fast how euer I doe sturre,
And now hath made me to his hand so right,
That in the manage I my selfe delight.

poems.title: Sonnet 49
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
STella, the fulnes cannot staied be
Of hidden thoughts, within my panting brest:
But they doe swell and struggle forth of me,
Till that in words thy figure be exprest;
And yet as soone as they thus formed be,
According to my Lord Loues owne behest,
With sad eyes I their weake proportion see
To portract what within this world is blest.
So that I cannot chuse but write my minde,
And cannot chuse but put out that I write,
While those poore babes their death in birth doe find;
And now my penne these lynes had dashed quite,
But that they stop his furie from the same:
Because their fore-front beares sweet Stellas name.

poems.title: Sonnet 50
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
PArdon mine eares, both I and they doe pray,
So may your tongue still flauntingly proceede,
To them that doe such entertainments neede;
So may you still haue something new to say
On sillie me, doe not your burthen lay
Of all the graue conceipts your braine doth breede:
But find some Hercules, to beare (in steede
Of Atlas tyrde) your wisedomes heauenly sway,
For me while you discourse of courtly tydes,
Of cunningst Fishers in most troubled streames,
Of straying waues when valiant errour guides;
Meane while my hart confers with Stellas beames,
As pittie tis so sweete a Comedie,
By such vnfitted speech, should hindered be.

poems.title: Sonnet 51
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
A Strife is growne betweene Vertue and Loue,
While each pretends, that Stella may be his:
Her eyes, her lips, Loue saith that he owes this,
Since they doe weare his badge, most firmely proue;
But Vertue thus, that title doth disproue.
That Stella, (ô deere name) that Stella is,
That vertuous Soule, sure heyre of heauenly Blisse:
Not this faire outside, which our hart doth moue;
And therefore, though her beauty and her grace,
Be Loues indeede, in Stellas selfe he may
By no pretence claime any manner place.
VVell Loue, since this Demurre our sute doth staie,
Let Vertue haue that Stellas selfe, yet thus,
That Vertue but that body graunt to vs.

poems.title: Sonnet 52
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
IN Martiall sports I had my cunning tryde,
And yet to breake more Staues I did adresse
VVhile people shoutes: indeede I must confesse,
Youth, luck, and praise, filled my vaines with pride;
When Cupid hauing me his slaue discride,
In Mars his liuerie, prauncing in the presse,
Now what sir foole said he (I would no lesse)
Looke heere I say, I lookt, and Stella spide:
Who hard by, through a window sent her light;
My hart then quakt, then daz'led were my eyes,
One hand forgot to rule, th'other to fight,
No Trumpet sound I heard, nor freendly cries;
My foe came on, and beate the ayre for mee,
Till that her blush, taught me my shame to see.

poems.title: Sonnet 53
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
BEcause I breathe not loue to euery one,
Nor doe not vse sette Colours for to weare:
Nor nourish speciall locks with vowed haire,
Nor giue each speech a full point of a grone,
The Courtly Nymphes acquainted with the mone
Of them, which in their lips Loues Standard beare:
What he, (say they of me) no I dare sweare,
He cannot loue: no, no, let him alone.
And thinke so still, so Stella know my minde.
Protest indeede, I know not Cupids dart:
But how faire Maides, at length this true shall find,
That his right badge, is learned in the hart.
Dumbe Swans, not chattering Pyes doe Louers proue,
They loue indeede, who dare not say they loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 54
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
FIE schoole of Patience, fie, your Lesson is
Far far too long, to learne it without booke:
What, a whole weeke, and get not halfe a looke?
And thinke I should not your large precepts misse,
VVhen I might reade these Letters fayre of blisse,
VVithin her face each vertue I could brooke,
From what the leaden counsels that I tooke:
As of a freende which meant not much amisse.
But now alas, that I doe want her sight,
What doost thou thinke that I can euertake,
In thy colde strife, a phlegmatick delight?
No Patience, if thou wilt my good, then make
Her come, and heere with patience my desire:
And then with patience bid me beare my fire.

poems.title: Sonnet 55
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
MVses, I oft haue crau'd your holy ayde,
With choisest flowres, my speech t'engarland so,
That it disguisde, in true (but naked) show,
Might winne some grace in your sweet skill arraide;
And oft whole troupes of saddest words I said,
Striuing abroade, a forraging to goe,
Vntill by your inspiring I might know,
How the blacke banners might be best displaid.
But I meane now no more your helpe to proue.
No other sugering of speech to try,
But on her name vncessantly to cry.
For let me but name her whom I doe loue,
So sweete sounde straight my eares and hart doe hit,
That I well finde no eloquence to it.

poems.title: Sonnet 56
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WOe hauing made with many sighs his owne
Each sence of mine; each gift, each power of minde
Growne now his slaues, he forst them out to finde
The throwest words, fit for Woes selfe to grone
Hoping that when they might finde Stella alone,
Before she could prepare to be vnkind,
Her soule (armed with such a daintie rinde,)
Should soone be hurt with sharpnes of the mone.
She heard my plaints, and did not onely heare,
But them so sweet, she did most sweetly sing,
With that faire brest, making Woes darknes cleere,
My priuie cares I holpe to her to bring,
To tell my griefe, and she with face and voice,
So sweetes my paines, that my paines me reioyce.

poems.title: Sonnet 57
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
DOubt there hath beene, when with his golden chaine
The Orator so farre mens harts doth bind:
That no place els their giddie steps could find;
But as he them more slacker short did raine,
Whether with words his sou'raigntie he gaine,
Clothed with fine tropes as his strongest linde,
Or els pronouncing grace, wherewith his minde
Prints his owne forme liuely, in rudest braine.
Now iudge by this, in pearcing phrases late
The Anatomie of all my woes I wrate,
Stellas sweete breath the same to me did reede.
Oh voyce, oh face, mauger my speeches might,
With wooed words, most rauishing delight,
Euen those sad words a ioy to me did breede.

poems.title: Sonnet 58
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney

poems.title: Sonnet 59
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
WHen my good Angell guides me to the place
Where's al my good; I doe in Stella see,
That Heauenly ioyes throwes onely downe on me
Thundred disdaines, and Lightning of disgrace;
But when the ruggedst step of Fortunes race
Makes me fall from her sight, then sweetly she
With words, wherein the Muses Treasures be,
Shewes loue and pittie to my absent case.
Now I (with beating long, by hardest fate)
So dull am, that I cannot looke into
The ground of this fierce loue, and louing hate;
Then some good body tell me how to do,
Whose presence absence, absence presence is:
Blest in my curse, and curssed in my blisse.

poems.title: Sonnet 60
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
OFt with true sighes, oft with vncalled teares,
Now with slow words, now with dumbe eloquence,
I Stellas eyes assailde, I closde her eares,
But this at last is her sweetest defence;
That who indeede a sound affection beares,
So captiues to his Saint both soule and mind,
That wholie Hers, all selfnes hee forbeares.
Thence his desire he learnes, his liues course thence,
Now since this chast loue, hates this loue in mee;
With chastned minde I needes must shew, that shee
Shall quickly me from what she hates remoue.
O Doctor Cupid, thou for me reply:
Driuen els to graunt by Angell Sophistry,
That I loue not, without I leaue to loue.

poems.title: Sonnet 61
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
LAte tyr'd with woe, euen ready for to pine
With rage of loue, I call my Loue vnkinde.
Shee in whose eyes, loues fyres vnfelt doe shine,
Sweetlie saide; I true loue in her shoulde finde.
I ioy, but straight thus watred was my wine:
That loue she did, but with a loue not blinde.
Which would not let me, whome she lou'd decline,
From Nobler course, fit for my birth and minde.
And therefore by her loues Authoritie;
Wilde me these Tempests of vaine loue to flee:
And Anchor fast my selfe on vertues shore.
Alas if this the onelie mettall be,
Of loue newe coyn'd to helpe my beggery:
Deere, loue me not, that you may loue me more.

poems.title: Sonnet 62
poems.author: Sir Philip Sidney
poems.text:
OH Grammer rules, oh now your vertues showe,
So Children still read you with awfull eyes,
As my younge Doue may in your precepts wise,
Her graunt to me by her owne vertue knowe.
For late with hart most hie, with eyes most lowe;
I crau'd the thing which euer she denies.
Shee lightening Loue, displaying Venus skyes,
Least one should not be heard twise, saide no no.
Harken Enuy not at my high triumphing:
But Grammers force with sweete successe confirme,
For Grammer sayes ah (this deere Stella way)
For Grammer sayes (to Grammer who sayes nay)
That in one speech, two negatiues affirme.
